title: The famous Venus of Willendorf is small enough to hold in one hand

cover.alt: The Venus of Willendorf: a small, rounded limestone figure of a nude woman with large breasts and belly, thin arms resting on her chest, and a head covered in rows of carved bands with no face.

body: This Stone Age figure of a woman was dug up on 7 August 1908 near the village of Willendorf in Lower Austria. It was carved about 30,000 years ago from oolitic limestone, tinted with red ochre, and it is tiny: just **11.1 cm** tall. It has no visible face, and like similar figures it probably never had feet, so it could not stand on its own, though it may have been pegged into soft ground. Research published in 2022 found that its stone most likely came from near Lake Garda in northern Italy, although a site in eastern Ukraine is also possible.

slides.question: How tall is the Venus of Willendorf?
slides.explanation: Just 11.1 cm (4.4 in): small enough to sit in the palm of your hand.

slides.alt: Four views of the Venus of Willendorf side by side, front, side, back and other side, showing the banded head from every angle.
slides.caption: Front, side, back, side. Her head is covered by rows that may be plaited hair, or perhaps a kind of headdress.

slides.heading: How old is it?
slides.note: Approximate. The Gravettian is the Stone Age culture the figure belongs to.

left.label: ‘Venus’
left.text: A modern nickname: archaeologists guessed the figure was a fertility goddess.

right.label: Really
right.text: It is many thousands of years older than the Roman goddess. It might be a fertility figure, or even a self-portrait. Nobody knows.

slides.heading: A stone from far away
slides.text: The 2022 study found the closest and most likely source of the oolite near Lake Garda in northern Italy. A lesser possibility is a site in eastern Ukraine, some 1,600 km away. Either way, it raises questions about how far people moved around in that age.

slides.heading: True or false?

items.text: It was tinted with red ochre
It has feet to stand on
The Romans named it after Venus

slides.explanation: It is oolitic limestone, it has no feet (it probably never had any), and ‘Venus’ is a modern name for a figure far older than Rome.
